name: Corticosteroid injection (Kenalog for cysts)

lead: Intralesional steroid injection places a small amount of a corticosteroid such as triamcinolone (Kenalog) directly into an inflamed acne lesion. Acne communities discuss it as a way to shrink and calm one large cyst or nodule quickly.

Triamcinolone is a potent glucocorticoid that reduces inflammation where it is placed, so swelling drops, the lesion flattens and redness fades. It has documented dermatologic uses, including keloid and hypertrophic scars, but no acne-cyst trials appear in the sources used here.

paras: It is done by a clinician for individual lesions and is an off-label use. It is aimed at single pimples rather than overall acne.

It is prescription-only. Documented effects from other injection routes include raised eye pressure and, with intravitreal use, rare endophthalmitis; systemic effects such as menstrual irregularity are listed by Wikipedia.

angle.text: A steroid injected into a single inflamed pimple lowers swelling and inflammation, so the cyst flattens and redness fades. Acne forum users describe it as a clinician-given quick fix, and it is an off-label procedure.

lead: Intralesional corticosteroid injection means injecting a small amount of a corticosteroid, most often triamcinolone acetonide (brand name Kenalog), directly into a skin lesion such as an inflamed acne nodule or cyst. Acne forums describe it as a way to reduce the size and redness of an individual pimple, and it is a clinician-administered procedure.[1]

Triamcinolone acetonide is a synthetic corticosteroid about eight times as potent as prednisone. Wikipedia lists intralesional injection for inflammation in skin lesions, notably hypertrophic and keloid scars, alongside joint, intravitreal, topical and nasal uses. It is prescription-only in the US, EU and UK.[1]
No trial of intralesional triamcinolone for acne cysts appears among the sources used here; registered studies of intralesional triamcinolone concern alopecia areata and keloids.[2][3][4]

paras: The practice discussed in appearance communities is injection of a dilute corticosteroid into an individual inflamed lesion. The sources cited here do not describe this acne use directly, so concentrations and technique are not covered.

Per Wikipedia, intralesional triamcinolone is used for inflammation within skin lesions, including hypertrophic and keloid scars; other uses include joint injections, intravitreal injections for macular edema, topical treatment, aphthous ulcers and allergic rhinitis sprays.[1]

Wikipedia notes that triamcinolone used for macular edema may raise intraocular pressure and that systemic effects include menstrual irregularities.[1] Ophthalmic studies of intravitreal triamcinolone also report raised eye pressure and, rarely, endophthalmitis.[5][6] These findings concern injection into the eye and are not studies of skin injection. Local skin atrophy and pigment loss are commonly named risks of intralesional steroids in dermatology, but they are not described in the sources cited here.
No studies found for intralesional corticosteroid injection of acne cysts in the sources used here.

Related registered studies of intralesional triamcinolone include a phase 2 study of Kenalog-10 in alopecia areata examining adrenal function (n=18)[2], a phase 2 study combining hyaluronic acid filler and triamcinolone for alopecia areata (n=14)[3], and a phase 4 trial of verapamil versus steroid to prevent keloid recurrence (terminated, n=14).[4] The registry records cited do not report results.
No community sources are cited for this entry.
